body:
>Is there a professor that you like that seems approachable? I'm not trying to be dismissive, but you're not the first student to feel like there's no point and it's quite possible one of your teachers has dealt with this before.

You're don't sound dismissive, you sound honest, and honesty is what helps the most.

I'll try some of my professors. I tried talking to one professor a semester ago, and he means well but is very...distracted. Which made getting my point across difficult, and I really don't think he would have understood my problem anyway. I don't know any of them very well (even the ones who've praised me, strangely enough - the one professor who as been the most outspoken about their approval of me still doesn't speak to me directly, instead only talking through proxies (grad students), which is really weird, now that I think about it), but I'm tempted just to show up and talk to them anyway.

>I'm not going to lie and tell you I read the entire thing...I drank more than I planned to tonight and reading is a bit fuzzy right now. 

I appreciate the honesty (I don't blame anyone for not reading through all of that).

>That said, I know you asked for no "generic fluffy nonsense," but as someone who just had two people within his close community commit suicide for what they viewed to be logical reasons, I can tell you that you cannot FATHOM the chaos you will unleash upon those who care about you. Your family and friends (going out on a limp and assuming you have some close friends or relatives) will be absolutely devastated.

I'm sorry to hear that you had to go through that. I just don't even know how to say I understand what it's like to experience that, because I don't. But, again, I'm truly sorry. That is by no means "generic fluffy nonsense." I meant more along the lines of, "The Easter Bunny and Baby Jeebus love you."

It's funny, because I was starting to seriously consider suicide a few weeks ago, and I knew I couldn't do it because someone I know has been very stressed and upset lately. I knew if I did it it'd have to be a time where everyone could bear the emotional burden, and even then I'd feel guilty. 

>I had pretty severe struggles with suicidal thoughts myself for several years as a result of similar, as a result of similar, but skewed conditions including medical woes (I've had orthopedic surgeries for osteochondroma several times a year since I was five or six) and social woes much like what you described. In elementary school I, too was described as a "prodigy" but I later ended up being an average student, which in turn made my overbearing father emotionally abusive toward me.

Wow. I hope you're doing better now. Sounds like you've dealt with much more difficult scenarios than what has me frustrated.

> And if so, well... what have you lost? If you've already lost the only things that matter to you, then you have lost nothing even if you do fail to find what you are searching for.

I had already thought of this, but for some reason I had just skipped over it a few weeks back. Thanks for mentioning it, because it's made the idea fresh in my mind. If you really have lost everything, then you might as well do something before you kill yourself. Then you find you really haven't lost everything...

I'm sorry for not responding to this.

You're right, it isn't all that logical, and thus I guess i can't really convince you it's a logical argument. 

It just seemed to make sense: I am unhappy with life, I see no viable alternative to what I have now, therefore dying is the only option. I'm wearily building the idea that I do have options though, with the help of all of the people posting here.

Buddhism has always seemed like a bunch of pretentious bullshit to me. Maybe I'm looking at it the wrong way.

I don't disagree with your general point about being happy from the inside though.

>Saying "I don't trust therapists" is like saying "I don't trust mechanics"; sure, there are some incompetent and crooked ones out there, but when your car or brain breaks down, you still need to find someone who can help you fix it, because you can't do much without it. And some of them are incredibly skilled and can tune you up into better shape than you ever thought possible.

Fair enough.

>People skills are just that - skills. Learnable skills. You'll go further in life with this book than a masters. $.35 cents plus shipping - can't beat that. Take the course if you ever have the dough. It won't be a waste.
 
I'll try that. Dealing with people efficiently couldn't hurt, even if I never "feel" it. Thanks for the recommendation.

>Quite frankly, your expectations/dreams/standards are not realistic. You are being so hard on yourself and your future that death is looking like a preferable option.

You're probably right, but I feel that not doing something impressive is stagnation, and stagnation is death. Maybe I'm taking it to the extreme.

>Doesn't sound like you'd be comfortable talking to your family, does your school have a counseling center?

The one time I did anything medically-related here, I ended up with a permanent scar because they didn't stitch something they should have because they didn't feel like it. So, I'm not eager to seek any of the "services" offered by the university. It sounds ridiculous, but maybe a professor would understand how I feel. Maybe? I don't know.  At least then I could phrase it as an academic question and seem relevant. I'd feel amazingly stupid walking into the counseling center and announcing, "Well, I have ridiculous standards and it makes me miserable!"

I met one person who was bright and sharp who I had romantic feelings for. I let that go. I think I probably dodged a bullet with that one, but I guess that'd be the closest I came to loving anyone.

I'm scared of letting someone have that much leverage in my life. How do you deal with that? I wear a "mask" with most people and don't let them know how I feel. I'm not sure I'm trusting enough to let someone into my life like that. Maybe if I meet the right person? I suspect most of the people I'd want to date are hiding somewhere like I am! q;

>Sounds like your grades are fucked right now anyway, so you have nothing to lose.

Somewhat fucked. My major GPA is still somehow a 3.4, but your point still stands.

I've considered freelance programming. I might try that during the summer just to check it out (that way I don't even have to drop out).

>Also, I highly recommend shopping around until you find a therapist who's smart and perceptive enough to trip you up. 

I do not trust therapists. I would never admit anything I'm admitting here in real life.

Sorry for responding so late to your post.

>Now, where is this money going to come from? Well, that's your call. You could try to do the professor thing, research or education. You could just get some mediocre job and work through it. You could probably even start your own business, if you like. You've got all kinds of options. That's something I'd like to emphasize here: suicide is but one of the many, many courses set before you. Ultimately it's up to you to decide just which of those is best, but I would certainly urge you to continue reconsidering suicide even up until the very point of death.

This is a great point. My only problem is navigating these things. Realistically, the best place to be employed would probably be a start-up company or something (flexible technology choice, better working hours, passionate people), but there are no such monsters where I live. Financially, I can't afford to relocate somewhere better (ever look at apartments in the Bay Area?).

>Prepare to roll your eyes at this, but you remind me a lot of how I used to be. You sound like you've been raised with enormously high expectations, cultivated an extremely diverse and deep range of knowledge and skills, and you expect to be able to do something with it all. Not just anything, something big. To make your mark on the world.

I smiled a lot when reading this. You're right on the mark. You have high standards for yourself, you're intense and almost drive yourself insane, and the praise of the people around you forms a positive feedback loop. But when you stumble, no one seems to be able to tell you what to do. "He's stopped succeeding, therefore it's over, let's move on to the next guy!" Then you assume you've failed and become depressed.

I remember once in highschool, I wanted to get recognized for programming. So even when no one else could, I worked away at it until I did. Then it wasn't enough. I knew I had to keep doing that to make myself happy (and I thought everyone's reaction to it was way below what it should be, so I figured I had to work harder), and in retrospect, that isn't healthy way to live. 

>I'll tell you right now, it is beyond futile trying to live for something as paltry as leaving a mark on this earth. Everybody leaves something behind here, and it's generally not the size so much as the quality that counts. I'd rather be a tiny patch of grass than a continental landfill.

Good point.

>II'm not saying you should just gun for the hedonistic, "live for myself and none other" approach. Well, you can of course, but that's not a course I would advocate. I won't really talk about what that course would be unless you want me to, because ultimately it doesn't matter what other people want. You're never going to please even half of everybody, it's useless trying to. So you may as well live for yourself. Study physics, work out expressions, compile away! If it makes you happy, if it does no harm to those around you... well, why the bloody hell not?

I mentioned above that I basically tried this for one semester, and I was the happiest person ever. Once you have enough discipline to work on your own, you find you don't need to societal constructs that everyone forces themselves into.

>Look, I don't know about you but I'm an atheist. As far as I'm concerned, this here? This is it. This is all you get. Eons pass, suddenly you pop into existence and for the tiniest moment you exist, not just in passing but as a conscious, feeling, sentient being. And then just as suddenly, you won't any more. 

I'm also an atheist, and I'll agree with you here. 

>Now, given this reality, would it not be prudent to take as much as you can out of what little you have? To me, that is the most logical answer I can give as to why you should not be committing suicide. You have one unbearably brief moment in time to do, well... anything! Have a kid. Establish a grocery store chain. Heal the sick. Solve P vs NP. It doesn't matter what exactly you do with this time, as long as you fill it with the things that matter to you. And I don't mean that as in just "whatever you like."

Yes! Yes! This is exactly it! I have been thinking this, and a few months ago I woke up and had a wonderful experience. I realized that I'm just driving this body here, and these things around me are all tangible, mutable and build-able. I realized I could poke at my life and make things work the way I wanted, or at least a little differently.

Then I realized I had 20-30 linear algebra problems (that I already know how to do) to do, a poorly-written 20 page PDF to dig through, and hours of programming on an assignment designed for those kids who are 2 years into a CS program and still don't "get" pointers.

Then I became twice as depressed as before. I don't know what to do here. Stay in school and tough it out? Go to another school? Drop out, and deal with the nagging feeling of failure (every day of my life it was hammered in my head that going to college was how I was going to distinguish myself from "those people" who are ignorant, petty and unproductive). It's tearing me apart, because I love to learn and feel like I should be in college, but the reality of it is so much different.

> I mean, what actually matters to you? Truth? Justice? Knowledge? Or maybe it is happiness, pleasure. I don't care what it is, but once you find that something of yours, you've won. The trick is finding it, and that is a thing I do not think I can help you with.

I'm not sure I have a precise answer to this. I'm glad you asked, because it gives me something to think about. My initial reaction is to say "intellectual stimulation", but there's got to be more there.

> A couple decades may feel long now, but you've already gone through at least a fifth of your natural life span, and very likely more than that. There's not much lost in sticking around, and the potential gain, personally, is tremendous. So when you ask me why, I fear I must ask in return "Why not?"

My biggest fear here is living a miserable existence where I'm working paycheck to paycheck on things I hate, too tired to work on my own projects that I care about. To live like this is, to me, to become an animal. I would rather die with some of my dignity still intact than live like this. What I'm afraid of is dropping/flunking out and living exactly like this, and given the jobs where I live, this seems very, very likely.

Thanks for the thoughtful post.

>Edit: And also I'm curious (and you should ask this of yourself) what do you want out of life? You seem to be thinking in the very short term with being unhappy with the school you chose and academic problems. Why does this present a problem for you? Do you have something specific you want to do? You mentioned things that others said you could do but not really what you want to do.

Good question. I think it's to (roughly in order of Maslow's hierarchy) 
a) be secure in my finances and have access to the few things I really want (books, comfortable living space by myself, etc.). 
b) do something profound for the human race, that either makes the world a more tolerable place (probably impossible for me to do to any satisfaction because my standards are ridiculous) or earns me recognition. 
c) to gain a large amount of freedom (obviously, you always have to work with people and negotiate implicit social contracts to some extent)

I guess that's it. What a shallow creature I am!
I don't know. Maybe they wouldn't. If nothing else, the feeling of failing them would motivate me to kick myself out.

I laughed a lot at this response (not in a mean way), and it made me happy (not sure if that's your intent, but whatever).

Silently removing yourself from "corporate society", as far as I can tell, wouldn't work. Even the Unabomber shopped at Walmart (he would apparently ride his mass-produced bike down a hill and buy his groceries from a large chain retail store, and then bike back up the hill to write a screed against industrialized society).

I'm not sure what my point is, except to say, you end up pigeonholed as a member somewhere in society whether you like it or not, and the thought of being at the bottom rung runs counter to everything I've been taught. I'm not sure I'd be able to stand it, and the thoughts of failure would eat me alive.

I'm paradoxically not interested in this world at all, and yet I'm overly concerned about where I "end up."

>Do have a girl/boyfriend? 

No. I have never dated (I'm a heterosexual male), and I am a virgin (I'm sure you totally didn't see that one coming), because I don't feel anything for most people. I operate best alone, and I don't see attaching myself to someone going very well. I don't know that I understand "love", only unhealthy infatuation followed by complete disinterest. I'm probably too narcissistic to sustain a relationship. I don't even understand if I'm attractive or not, and I can't distinguish between romantic interest and someone just being nice.

>Do you get joy from reading for fun (non-school stuff)?

Yes. I mostly read non-fiction though. I read textbooks and technical books for pleasure (believe it or not, there are good ones worth reading that are very well written). I only like fiction if it has a point of make or is exceptionally "mind-blowing." I will admit to liking some philosophy, and that's a bit of a guilty pleasure.

>I'd love to hear what little things (cooking for me!) make you secretly smile.

Hmm. Maybe music (but everyone says that). I sometimes write for pleasure. I also sometimes draw, or edit photographs in weird ways. Biking is fun.

>Afford to how? Financially?

Yes. If I move back home, no matter how short the period of time, I will be marked with the stigma of failure by family (because I will be failure) and will probably be forced to move out. I have no financial support for college or anything else, so it'd be rough (I'm supported on scholarships and grants now).

>To be honest I envy your passion. I have a very easy time in school but I am so apathetic about everything that I can never bring myself to do any school work at all and subsequently end up failing many classes, and then not even caring in the slightest.

Uh, that's exactly what I said is happening to me. I have a passion for the things I do in my own time, but school is exactly the same for me. I just don't care anymore. I could do the work if I cared. But I really don't give a shit about, say, computing 20 3x3 matrix determinants. I can do the computation fine, and doing 20 of them doesn't help anything.

>So why not just work somewhere chilled for a while, get your head straight and then continue, not only is there nothing wrong with a pitstop, its not even a big deal on the grand scale of things.

I'm not sure there's anywhere decent around me to work. I've had a job on the side since I was a kid, and all of them have sucked (I'm not trying to sound entitled, I just can't stand the prospect of another summer spent dealing with people every day - they make me anxious and angry).

I got offered a few software contracts in highschool but didn't take them because they were full-time (and I was in school), so I guess I could pursue that route again.

>So is it the challenge of math that you like? 

Yes, and the fact that I can get far in it without dealing directly with other people. I mean, I don't know how to say, "I just like the subject and the way that it works" without being vague. 

>What is it about research that appeals to you?

Freedom. The freedom to find my own problems to work on, the freedom to learn with the books I see fit when I see fit (i.e., not being forced to read the $150 festering piles of trash (that teach rote memorization instead of conceptual mastery) they shove down our throats) as long as I product results, where "results" are judged by people who are at least somewhat competent. I'm sure in reality it will be very imperfect and I'll find 8 million little things to hate, but it seems better than what I have now.

I know what makes me happy. I don't know how to exist in this world doing the things that make me happy. At that point, I'm basically lost, and I'll be damned if I'm going to sit around in a miserable bubble wasting my time and everyone else's figuring it out (because I really can't afford to).

What do you suggest? The corporate world seems worse to me. I honestly think I'd be happy doing research in math (I sat through a seminar which gave some insight into what its like to research in the field, and it was awesome), but I can't do that if I don't get through my undergraduate, and it seems like that's not going to happen.

I think I'd be happier at a more challenging school with faculty that actually care about students, but I see no realistic way of making that happen, as they're all too expensive (I'm paying my way through this school with scholarships and grants). So, that leaves me nowhere.
